title: Sandboxed mini-runway: SDK bootstrapping playbook (sketch)
content:
Purpose:
This sketch documents a compact, low-friction onramp we can ship as a playground-style lab for new SDK adopters. The goal is to get an engineer from repo checkout -> instrumented sample app -> validated telemetry within 20–30 minutes, all inside a sandboxed flow that demonstrates the platform features that matter most for production: low-latency streaming, fallbacks, and simple cost controls.

Audience:
- New hires in product/plat dev teams trying Redwood SDKs
- External integrators evaluating Redwood for a prototype
- Solutions engineers running a 1:1 lab with customers

High-level goals (success metrics):
- Time-to-first-successful-request <= 15 minutes for 75% of users in lab run
- Telemetry (latency, token counts, error rate) visible in the sample app dashboard within 30 minutes
- Clear path to a canary rollout: SDK hooks + sample config for feature flags and fallback policies

Non-goals:
- Full production hardening (this is a sandbox sketch)
- Full enterprise onboarding (SAML/KMS) — those are separate playbooks

Core narrative (short):
1) Clone minimal sample repo (polyglot examples: node, python, go).
2) Run local sandbox script that 1) spins a tiny mock server, 2) provisions a short-lived API key bound to the lab workspace, 3) preloads a prompt corpus for tests.
3) Execute three guided flows: quick generate, streaming chat with function-call demo, and embeddings + rerank flow.
4) Open the lightweight telemetry UI (bundled) to inspect token usage and latency.
5) Introduce a simple failure/cutover experiment: trigger a model timeout -> automatic fallback to cheaper model + show how the SDK surface exposes the event.

Lab constraints and choices:
- Keep hardware/environment simple: local dev machine + Docker. No GPU required (use small open model container or mock service).
- Telemetry should be lightweight: emit JSON-lines to a file and include a tiny web UI to parse and visualize.
- Use short-lived API keys to avoid long-lived secrets in examples.
- Provide a single command that runs the whole setup (bootstrap.sh / bootstrap.ps1).

Detailed steps (developer-facing):
- Step 0: prerequisites: git, node 18+, python 3.10, docker (optional)
- Step 1: git clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-examples && cd sdk-examples/mini-runway
- Step 2: ./bootstrap.sh (creates .env with SAMPLE_KEY, starts mock backend if docker available)
- Step 3: npm install && npm run start:sample (or python3 -m sample_app)
- Step 4: Visit http://localhost:3000/mini-runway to see the sample app with three tabs: Generate, Chat, Embeddings
- Step 5: Run the quick test suite: npm run test:smoke (asserts 3 success cases and writes telemetry jsonl)

What the sample app shows (learning moments):
- Streaming generation vs. batch: show latency differences with measured timestamps.
- KV/cache effect: run a pair of requests where second reuses prefix and shows reduced tokens billed and lower latency.
- Fallback policy: intentionally block the primary model and show automatic switch to compatible variant; log the switch in telemetry and show how to configure policy in a single JSON file.
- Cost estimate card: simple per-request token cost estimate based on model profile (illustrative).

Telemetry contract (minimal):
Each request emits a JSON line with: request_id, route, model, model_variant, start_ts, end_ts, token_input, token_output, status, fallback_triggered (bool), error_code (if any)
We will ship parsers for these logs inside the mini-runway UI. The sample UI will also show aggregate metrics: p50/p95 latency, requests/min, token/min.

Gating & rollout checks for this doc:
- Must have reproducible bootstrap on macOS and Linux.
- Smoke test must pass in CI on PRs to the example repo (CI job runs bootstrap + smoke tests).
- UX: pages should have clear next steps and a short checklist for moving to Dedicated/Private (what changes: keys, telemetry endpoints, KMS).

Failure modes to highlight (teachable moments):
- Network flakiness: show retry/backoff policy and how SDK surfaces retry counters.
- Cold KV cache: show a first-request penalty and how caching mitigates it.
- Token explosion: show a malformed prompt that causes large output and how to attach output limits and graceful truncation.

Developer experience hooks (API surfaces we want to exercise):
- init(config) — show quick config options for model selection, fallback policy, and telemetry endpoint.
- stream(handler) — minimal streaming handler example to render tokens as they arrive.
- withTelemetrySpan() — wrapper to create spans for a request lifecycle (used by the sample UI to link client traces to telemetry).
- offlineStub() — local stub mode for disconnected demos.

Checklist for the engineering owner (MVP for the lab):
- [ ] Minimal polyglot samples implemented (node + python + go)
- [ ] bootstrap script that provisions sample key and mock backend
- [ ] telemetry jsonl parser + tiny web UI in repo
- [ ] CI smoke job wired for PRs
- [ ] README with 15-min checklist and instructor notes for Solutions Eng 
- [ ] Failure-mode scenarios scripted as test cases
- [ ] Example fallback policy JSON and quick guide on model variants map

Instructor notes (for SE running a 1:1 lab):
- Walk the user through the Generate tab first — quick wins
- After successful generate, run the streaming chat to show latency/UX difference
- Intentionally flip the mock backend to simulate a model outage and walk through the fallback behavior and logs
- End by pointing to the path-to-prod doc and the dedicated onboarding checklist (SAML/KMS)

Open questions / unknowns (to resolve before we call this final):
- How far do we go with the mock backend vs. a tiny containerized open model? (tradeoff: realism vs. reproducibility)
- Should the sample telemetry UI push to an ephemeral cloud staging dashboard for instructors, or keep entirely local?
- Do we include an embeddings playground tied to a tiny reranker example (adds more value but more surface area)?

Next steps (concrete):
1) Engineering: spin up a spike to implement the Node flow + bootstrap in 2 sprints (owner: Evan)
2) DevExp: draft the 15-min README and SE instructor script (owner: Maya)
3) Solutions Eng: run three internal labs and capture failure notes (owner: Priya)

Notes to self: keep friction lower than 3 commands. The magic is the guided narrative — not exhaustive config. Aim for delight on first contact.
